newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Malaysia to buy more corn after 100,000T purchase.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia to buy more corn after 100,000T purchase.

text.p: Malaysia has purchased up to 100,000 tonnes of corn for February and March deliveries with the bulk of the imports from China and is in the market to buy more if prices are attractive, trade sources said on Thursday.
"Malaysia has purchased about 100,000 tonnes of corn for February and March and most of this corn is of Chinese origin," said a trader with a European firm.
"The U.S prices are not attractive enough for the Malaysian buyers compared to the Chinese offers," he said.
"A 10,000 tonne cargo of Chinese corn for delivery to Malaysia is currently offered at $147-$149 (C&F) a tonne against bids at $145-$146," the trader added.
China eased its Decmber 1994 ban on corn exports recently and is estimated to have anything between one and two million tonnes of corn for sale.
Chinese sellers have already secured sales to South Korea and are actively offering in the Philippines and Indonesia.
Traders said Malaysia is still in the market to buy more if prices are attractive.
"Malaysia has a lot of local corn stored in the warehouses in west Malaysia but that will be depleted soon and the new shipments will not be sufficient to last them very long," one trader said.
"They are likely to start buying after February when the Chinese and Moslim festivities are over," he said.
Traders said while there are pockets of demand seen in the Southeast Asian grain market, there are still adequate supplies so far to meet that demand.
"The Chinese corn is just filling the supply gap before the regional supplies from Indonesia and Thailand come in later in March or April," said another trader.
"By then, you'll probably seen these supplies struggling for market share with the Argentine bags," he added.
Traders said Argentine supplies have been offered in the market at between $140-$145 against bids at $138-$139 a tonne.
They said Thai buyers have been staying at the sidelines. "While some inquiries were heard, there were no transactions," said one trader.
Indian soymeal prices were stable but bid/offer indications were far apart. "There is hardly any activity," one trader said.
Traders said Indian soymeal for delivery in February or March was quoted at $308-$312 a tonne C&F.

"The market has become very quiet after the recent diversions of large amounts of soymeal from the congested ports in China to Southeast Asia seen earlier this month," said the trader with the European firm.
"While stocks in India are quite tight at the moment there is no huge (soymeal) demand emerging in the region to spur prices upwards," he said. "Prices are high enough," he said.
"We may see some demand from Indonesia but I think buyers in Thailand and Malaysia have already purchased enough," he said.
"Most buyers are covered until March," said another trader.
